chapter: Probation, Las Vegas and Los Angeles in the 1950s
title: Stranded after the closing: free meals, $18 from the union, never paid
summary: Performers were fed in the dining room; the union gave $18 to leave town and the debt was never paid.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I know they had announced a fantastic lineup of stars they were going to have there.

Yeah. Well, the results now, after they closed up the place, all of these performers didn't have any money to eat on, so the hotel served free meals to the performers and the musicians, and we all had to be in the dining room on time. If you missed a meal you couldn't come back and say, 'I'm hungry.' It wasn't like that. You had to be there and sit down and eat, everyone at the same time. So we're trying to get some money to get out of town, you know, a part of our money that was due us. And we didn't know which way to go, so we went to the union, and Harry Sweets Edison drove his Cadillac to the union and Kolax Coleax is sitting in the co-pilot's seat and I'm in the back seat. The union -- it was very large of them -- they collect more tax than anyplace in the United States, in Las Vegas, you know, off of entertainment. And they gave everyone $18.00, which was no more than a plane ride to Los Angeles at that time. That was as far as you could come. All they wanted you to do was get out of Las Vegas and then you could take care of your business from Los Angeles and try to get back to where you come from. But I came back on that $18.00, came back and got my automobile, took my bass home, got my clothes and brought enough clothes for three days and came
So you never got your money.

No. First they said, 'Well, we'll give it to a hospital and let them make a hospital out of it.' There's plenty of space there, you know, if they rearrange it properly they could have had a whole lot of rooms there, hospital wise. And they didn't do that. Then they said they was going to have it as a lecture hall, the main dining room, was going to use it for lecturing, you know. What type of lecturing, don't ask me. And for conventions. Speaking of having it as a convention headquarters for whoever came there and didn't want to live on the strip, they could come there and live cheaper, you know. So, as a result, they just closed the whole thing down. Now, in later years, the hotel part and the annex is open, but the casino and the main dining room isn't. So no-one's liable for our debt.
